what_its_for: Decitabine is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat a blood and bone marrow condition called myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). MDS is a group of disorders where your bone marrow does not make enough healthy blood cells. This medicine works by helping cancer cells become more normal and by slowing or stopping the growth of abnormal cells.
how_to_take: Decitabine is given as an IV (intravenous) infusion — meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or doctor will give you this medicine in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT take this medicine at home as a pill. Each infusion usually takes about 1 to 3 hours. You will receive treatments in cycles, with rest periods in between to allow your body to recover.
dosing: Your doctor will decide your exact dose based on your body size (height and weight), kidney and liver function, and your overall health. A common schedule is once daily for 5 days in a row, followed by a 3-week rest period — this makes up one treatment cycle. Another schedule may be given over 3 days every 6 weeks. Your doctor may adjust your dose if you have side effects or if your blood counts are too low. Always follow the exact schedule your doctor or nurse gives you.
missed_dose: Because decitabine is given by a healthcare team in a clinic or hospital, you will have scheduled appointments for each dose. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away. Do not try to 'make up' a missed dose on your own. Your doctor will decide the best plan to get you back on schedule safely.
storage: You do not store this medicine at home — it is prepared and kept by the pharmacy or healthcare team at the clinic or hospital. If you are ever given any supplies related to your treatment to keep at home, store them exactly as instructed by your pharmacist or nurse, typically in a cool, dry place away from children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, since decitabine lowers your immune system and makes it easier for you to get sick. Avoid live vaccines (such as the nasal flu spray) while on treatment — ask your doctor before getting any vaccine. Avoid alcohol or limit it, as it can worsen side effects. Women who are pregnant or could become pregnant should avoid handling this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for several months after. Men should also use birth control during and after treatment. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Avoid crowds and people with colds, flu, or other illnesses whenever possible.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, chills, or signs of infection; unusual bleeding or bruising; extreme tiredness or weakness; shortness of breath or chest pain; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control; swelling of your hands, feet, or ankles; signs of low blood sugar (shaking, sweating, fast heartbeat, confusion); redness, pain, or swelling at your IV site; or any new or worsening symptoms that worry you. Do not wait — infections and bleeding can become life-threatening quickly during chemotherapy.
when_it_works: Decitabine may take several treatment cycles before you notice improvement. Many patients begin to respond after 2 to 4 cycles (which can take 2 to 6 months). Your doctor will check your blood counts and bone marrow regularly to see how the medicine is working. Do not get discouraged if you do not feel better right away — some patients need more time to respond. Keep all of your scheduled appointments and blood tests so your doctor can monitor your progress.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Decitabine can seriously harm an unborn baby. Do not become pregnant during treatment. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after your last dose. Older adults (65 and older): Older patients can receive this medicine, but may need closer monitoring for side effects like infections and fatigue. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor will monitor your kidney and liver function and may adjust your dose if needed. Children: The safety and effectiveness of decitabine in children has not been fully established. Talk to your child's doctor for guidance.
